claim: 23% of pure tone audiograms from 132,504 case records at Massachusetts Eye and Ear audiology clinic fit the description of high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL).
source: We reviewed 132,504 case records from visitors to the audiology clinic at our institution and determined that 23% of pure tone audiograms fit the description of high-frequency SNHL (Figure 1A)
evidence: Based on analysis of clinical database records and shown in Figure 1A

claim: High-frequency SNHL is commonly related to tinnitus, abnormal loudness growth, and poor speech intelligibility in noise.
source: underscoring that it is a common clinical condition commonly related to tinnitus, abnormal loudness growth, and poor speech intelligibility in noise (Horwitz et al., 2002; Lewis et al., 2020; Moore et al., 1999; Oxenham and Bacon, 2003; Strelcyk and Dau, 2009)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Exposure to narrow-band high-frequency noise (16–32 kHz) at 103 dB SPL for 2 hr induces sustained elevation of high-frequency thresholds for ABR wave 1 and DPOAEs in mice.
source: Repeated cochlear function testing before and after noise exposure revealed a sustained elevation of high-frequency thresholds for wave 1 of the auditory brainstem response (ABR) and cochlear distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs) with mild or no threshold elevation below 16 kHz (Figure 1B, C)
evidence: Demonstrated through repeated cochlear function testing shown in Figures 1B and 1C

claim: High-frequency noise exposure eliminated approximately 50% of synaptic contacts between inner hair cells (IHCs) and primary cochlear afferent neurons in the high-frequency base of the cochlea.
source: Compared to age-matched unexposed control ears, high-frequency noise exposure eliminated approximately 50% of synaptic contacts between inner hair cells (IHCs) and primary cochlear afferent neurons in the high-frequency base of the cochlea (Figure 1D)
evidence: Based on post-mortem cochlear histopathology performed 21 days after noise exposure, shown in Figure 1D

claim: Noise-induced outer hair cell (OHC) death was only observed in the high-frequency extreme of the cochlear base.
source: Noise-induced outer hair cell (OHC) death was only observed in the high-frequency extreme of the cochlear base (Figure 1E)
evidence: Based on cochlear histopathology data shown in Figure 1E

claim: More subtle OHC stereocilia damage was evident throughout mid- and high-frequency cochlear regions after noise exposure.
source: though more subtle OHC stereocilia damage was evident throughout mid- and high-frequency cochlear regions (Figure 1F, G)
evidence: Based on cochlear histopathology visualized in Figures 1F and 1G

claim: Traumatic noise exposure resulted in a stable 45 dB increase in high-frequency tone threshold without commensurate changes in false alarm rates or mid-frequency detection thresholds.
source: revealing a stable 45 dB increase in high-frequency tone threshold after traumatic noise exposure without commensurate changes in false alarm rates or mid-frequency detection thresholds (Figure 1J, K, statistical analyses are provided in figure legends)
evidence: Based on behavioral detection thresholds measured every 1–3 days before and after noise-induced SNHL, shown in Figures 1J and 1K

claim: Following acoustic trauma, the behavioral sensitivity index (d-prime) grew more steeply for sound intensities near threshold for the spared 8 kHz tone compared to pre-exposure baseline and sham-exposed controls.
source: This analysis confirmed that, following acoustic trauma, the behavioral sensitivity index (d-prime, or d′) grew more steeply for sound intensities near threshold compared both to pre-exposure baseline detection functions and sham-exposed controls (Figure 2A, B)
evidence: Based on analysis of psychometric detection functions shown in Figures 2A and 2B

claim: An increase in psychometric growth slopes by at least 30% from baseline was observed in 7/7 acoustic trauma mice but not in any sham-exposed control mice.
source: These effects were consistent at the level of individual mice, where we noted an increase in psychometric growth slopes by at least 30% from baseline in 7/7 acoustic trauma mice but changes of this magnitude were not observed in any sham-exposed control mice (Figure 2B, right)
evidence: Based on individual mouse data shown in Figure 2B right panel

claim: Mice with high-frequency SNHL exhibited behavioral hypersensitivity to direct optogenetic stimulation of auditory thalamocortical neurons.
source: Importantly, testing in interleaved trials revealed behavioral hypersensitivity to direct stimulation of auditory thalamocortical neurons after acoustic trauma (Figure 2E), as evidenced by significantly increased d′ at a fixed set of optogenetic stimulation intensities compared to sham controls (Figure 2F)
evidence: Based on interleaved acoustic and optogenetic stimulation testing shown in Figures 2E and 2F

claim: Tonotopic maps were relatively stable over ~4 weeks in mice with normal hearing experience.
source: These experiments confirmed that tonotopic maps were relatively stable over ~4 weeks in mice with normal hearing experience (Issa et al., 2014; Romero et al., 2019)
evidence: Confirmed through widefield epifluorescence calcium imaging and supported by prior citations

claim: Tonotopic maps underwent large-scale reorganization throughout the week following acoustic trauma before stabilizing in a state that over-represented 8–16 kHz tones that bordered the high-frequency cochlear lesion.
source: but underwent large-scale reorganization throughout the week following acoustic trauma before stabilizing in a state that over-represented 8–16 kHz tones that bordered the high-frequency cochlear lesion (Figure 3B)
evidence: Based on chronic widefield calcium imaging shown in Figure 3B

claim: Individual L2/3 PyrNs exhibited strong tone-evoked transients and well-organized tonal receptive fields.
source: Individual L2/3 PyrNs exhibited strong tone-evoked transients and well-organized tonal receptive fields (Figure 3D)
evidence: Based on two-photon cellular-scale measurements shown in Figure 3D

claim: Tonotopic remapping was limited to the deafferented zone.
source: Analysis of all tone-responsive PyrNs (n = 1749 in four trauma mice; n = 1748 in four sham mice) demonstrated that tonotopic remapping was limited to the deafferented zone (Figure 3G)
evidence: Based on analysis of all tone-responsive PyrNs shown in Figure 3G

claim: The percentage of L2/3 PyrNs preferentially tuned to lesion edge frequencies more than doubled following acoustic trauma in the deafferented zone.
source: where the percentage of L2/3 PyrNs preferentially tuned to lesion edge frequencies more than doubled following acoustic trauma (Figure 3H)
evidence: Based on analysis shown in Figure 3H

claim: Tonotopic remapping occurred without any systematic change in response threshold.
source: without any systematic change in response threshold (Figure 3I)
evidence: Based on threshold analysis shown in Figure 3I

claim: Neural gain was broadly enhanced across the tonotopic map for the first several days following trauma but then receded to the high-frequency deafferented region in measurements made 1 week or more following noise exposure.
source: We noted that neural gain was broadly enhanced across the tonotopic map for the first several days following trauma but then receded to the high-frequency deafferented region in measurements made 1 week or more following noise exposure (Figure 5B)
evidence: Based on neural gain analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: A strong initial uptick in neural gain was measured in both topographic regions following trauma.
source: This analysis identified several clear results: (1) a strong initial uptick in neural gain measured in both topographic regions following trauma
evidence: Based on neural gain analysis across four stimulus frequencies

claim: Persistent (lasting greater than 1 week) increases in neural gain were observed only for spared mid-frequency tones in deafferented cortical regions.
source: (2) persistent (lasting greater than 1 week) increases in neural gain were observed only for spared mid-frequency tones in deafferented cortical regions
evidence: Based on neural gain analysis across four stimulus frequencies

claim: No significant changes in neural gain were observed in sham-exposed mice.
source: (3) no significant changes in neural gain were observed in sham-exposed mice (Figure 5C)
evidence: Based on neural gain analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: Excess gain in A1 L2/3 PyrNs reflected the interaction of four factors: whether the initial sound exposure induced SNHL, where within the cortical frequency map the cell is located, when relative to exposure the measurement is made, and the proximity of the stimulus test frequency to the cochlear lesion.
source: Thus, excess central gain reflected the interaction of four factors: (1) whether the initial sound exposure induced SNHL, (2) where within the cortical frequency map the cell is located, (3) when relative to exposure the measurement is made, and (4) the proximity of the stimulus test frequency to the cochlear lesion
evidence: Based on comprehensive neural gain analysis across multiple factors

claim: Enhanced neural detection of 8 kHz tones was largely driven by PyrNs in deafferented map regions.
source: Enhanced neural detection of 8 kHz tones was largely driven by PyrNs in deafferented map regions, whereas the loss of cortical sensitivity to high-frequency tones was observed in both topographic zones (Figure 5F)
evidence: Based on SVM decoder analysis shown in Figure 5F

claim: An approximate 20% increase in PyrN spontaneous activity across A1 was noted after acoustic trauma, but relatively modest effects following sham exposure.
source: Normalizing by the pre-exposure period, we noted an approximate 20% increase in PyrN spontaneous activity across A1 after acoustic trauma, but relatively modest effects following sham exposure (Figure 7A, B)
evidence: Based on spontaneous activity analysis shown in Figures 7A and 7B

claim: Increased spontaneous activity after acoustic trauma was not topographically restricted and continued to increase steadily with time after acoustic trauma.
source: Unlike the increase in edge frequency tone-responsiveness, increased spontaneous activity after acoustic trauma was not topographically restricted and continued to increase steadily with time after acoustic trauma (Figure 7B, C)
evidence: Based on spontaneous activity analysis shown in Figures 7B and 7C

claim: Synchronized activity normally decayed to asymptote once PyrNs were separated by more than 0.25 mm.
source: Using the area under the shuffle-corrected cross-correlogram as our index of pairwise synchrony (Figure 7D), we noted that synchronized activity normally decayed to asymptote once PyrNs were separated by more than 0.25 mm (Figure 7E, top)
evidence: Based on cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E top panel

claim: In the first 72 hr following acoustic trauma, pairwise synchrony was significantly enhanced for PyrNs separated by as much as 0.7 mm.
source: In the first 72 hr following acoustic trauma, pairwise synchrony was significantly enhanced for PyrNs separated by as much as 0.7 mm (Figure 7E, bottom)
evidence: Based on cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E bottom panel

claim: Three days after trauma and beyond, local synchrony remained strongly elevated for PyrNs relative both to baseline and to sham-exposed controls.
source: Three days after trauma and beyond, local synchrony remained strongly elevated for PyrNs relative both to baseline and to sham-exposed controls
evidence: Based on cross-correlation analysis over time

claim: Increased synchrony following trauma was primarily observed in PyrN's located close to – or straddling – the deafferentation boundary, where the peak of elevated synchrony was positioned within a tonotopic region corresponding to lesion edge sound frequencies.
source: Increased synchrony following trauma was primarily observed in PyrN's located close to – or straddling – the deafferentation boundary, where the peak of elevated synchrony was positioned within a tonotopic region corresponding to lesion edge sound frequencies (Figure 7F)
evidence: Based on topographic analysis of synchrony shown in Figure 7F

claim: Plasticity following acoustic trauma is organized into two phases: a dynamic phase during the first 48–72 hr after noise exposure involving topographically widespread hyper-correlation, hyper-responsivity to mid-frequency sounds in the intact map regions, and large-scale turnover in PyrN stability around the deafferentation map boundary, followed by a stable phase beginning 3 days after exposure where gain is increased for spared tone frequencies in deafferented map regions.
source: Taken together, these observations also suggest that plasticity following acoustic trauma is organized into two phases: a dynamic phase during the first 48–72 hr after noise exposure involving topographically widespread hyper-correlation, hyper-responsivity to mid-frequency sounds in the intact map regions, and large-scale turnover in PyrN stability around the deafferentation map boundary, followed by a stable phase beginning 3 days after exposure where gain is increased for spared tone frequencies in deafferented map regions
evidence: Based on synthesis of multiple observations from chronic imaging experiments

claim: New active PyrNs appeared immediately following noise exposure, while PyrNs tracked throughout the baseline imaging sessions disappeared.
source: Interestingly, we noted that new active PyrNs appeared immediately following noise exposure, while PyrNs tracked throughout the baseline imaging sessions disappeared (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Based on chronic cell tracking analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Approximately 75% of PyrN disappearance occurred within the 48 hr after acoustic trauma.
source: and because approximately 75% of PyrN disappearance occurred within the 48 hr after acoustic trauma (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Based on analysis of PyrN turnover shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E

claim: Excess non-homeostatic gain regulation following acoustic trauma occurred with the highest probability in PyrNs exhibiting weak, monotonically increasing 8 kHz growth functions and higher spontaneous activity levels at baseline.
source: We observed that excess non-homeostatic gain regulation following acoustic trauma occurred with the highest probability in PyrNs exhibiting weak, monotonically increasing 8 kHz growth functions and higher spontaneous activity levels at baseline (Figure 8G)
evidence: Based on linear regression model results shown in Figure 8G

claim: PyrNs located in the high-frequency (deafferented) region but with a lower frequency BF further increased the likelihood of expressing excess neural gain after trauma.
source: Further, PyrNs located in the high-frequency (deafferented) region but with a lower frequency BF further increased the likelihood of expressing excess neural gain after trauma (Figure 8G)
evidence: Based on linear regression model results shown in Figure 8G

claim: Certain idiosyncratic response features measured just prior to acoustic trauma can predict whether A1 L2/3 PyrNs will undergo stable, homeostatic regulation or excess, non-homeostatic changes to a stimulus positioned near the edge of the cochlear lesion.
source: This suggests that while cortical gain changes are triggered by reduced bottom-up afferent input, their subsequent stabilization is also shaped by their local circuit milieu, where indicators of reduced inhibition can presage pathological hyperactivity following sensorineural hearing loss
evidence: Based on synthesis of predictive modeling results

claim: Behavioral hypersensitivity to spared mid-frequency tones was observed for direct stimulation of thalamocortical projection neurons, identifying the ACtx as a potential locus of plasticity underlying auditory hypersensitivity.
source: We demonstrated that behavioral hypersensitivity to spared, mid-frequency tones was also observed for direct stimulation of thalamocortical projection neurons, identifying the ACtx as a potential locus of plasticity underlying auditory hypersensitivity (Figure 2)
evidence: Based on combined acoustic and optogenetic behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2

claim: Neural hyperresponsivity to spared mid-frequency sounds was accompanied by hyperactive and hyper-correlated spontaneous activity.
source: Neural hyperresponsivity to spared mid-frequency sounds was accompanied by hyperactive and hyper-correlated spontaneous activity (Figure 7)
evidence: Based on spontaneous activity and correlation analyses shown in Figure 7

claim: The degree of excess neural gain following acoustic trauma in individual neurons could be predicted from many response features measured during the pre-exposure baseline period.
source: where the degree of excess neural gain following acoustic trauma in individual neurons could be predicted from many of these response features measured during the pre-exposure baseline period (Figure 8)
evidence: Based on predictive modeling shown in Figure 8

claim: Excess central gain is the hypothesized neural substrate of auditory hypersensitivity.
source: Excess central gain – an abnormally steep growth of neural response with sound intensity – is the hypothesized neural substrate of auditory hypersensitivity (Auerbach et al., 2019, Auerbach et al., 2014; Zeng, 2020; Zeng, 2013)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Excess central gain is prominently expressed in the ACtx of animals with sensorineural cochlear damage.
source: Excess central gain is prominently expressed in the ACtx of animals with sensorineural cochlear damage (Asokan et al., 2018; Chambers et al., 2016a; Noreña et al., 2003; Parameshwarappa et al., 2022; Popelár et al., 1987; Qiu et al., 2000; Resnik and Polley, 2017, Resnik and Polley, 2021; Seki and Eggermont, 2003; Syka et al., 1994)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: In the auditory nerve, sound-evoked neural responses are strongly reduced after sensorineural cochlear damage.
source: by contrast to the auditory nerve, where sound-evoked neural responses are strongly reduced (Heinz et al., 2005; Heinz and Young, 2004; Wake et al., 1993)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Reorganization is observed in subcortical stations of sound processing in animals with sensorineural cochlear damage, but only in particular cell types and is less robust overall than neural gain changes at the level of ACtx.
source: Reorganization is also observed in subcortical stations of sound processing in animals with sensorineural cochlear damage (Chambers et al., 2016b; Kamke et al., 2003; Niu et al., 2013; Schrode et al., 2018; Shaheen and Liberman, 2018), but only particular cell types (Cai et al., 2009) and – in studies that have made direct inter-regional comparisons – is less robust overall than neural gain changes at the level of ACtx (Chambers et al., 2016a; Qiu et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Changes in ACtx gene expression after cochlear damage result in elevated mRNA levels for glutamate receptor subunits and reduced mRNA transcripts and membrane-bound protein expression for GABAA receptor units.
source: Hypersensitivity to direct stimulation of the thalamocortical pathway may be underpinned by changes in ACtx gene expression that result in elevated mRNA levels for glutamate receptor subunits and reduced mRNA transcripts and membrane-bound protein expression for GABAA receptor units (Balaram et al., 2019; Sarro et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Adjustments in ligand-gated receptors have been associated with commensurate elevations in spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents and reduced inhibitory postsynaptic currents in PyrNs.
source: These adjustments in ligand-gated receptors have been associated with commensurate elevations in spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents and reduced inhibitory postsynaptic currents in PyrNs (Kotak et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Disinhibition and hypersensitization are conceptualized as synergistic compensatory responses that are triggered by a sudden decline in peripheral neural input, rendering cortical PyrNs less sensitive to feedforward inhibition from local inhibitory neurons and hyperresponsive to sound.
source: Thus, disinhibition and hypersensitization are conceptualized as synergistic compensatory responses that are triggered by a sudden decline in peripheral neural input, rendering cortical PyrNs less sensitive to feedforward inhibition from local inhibitory neurons – from parvalbumin-expressing (PV) fast-spiking interneurons in particular – and hyperresponsive to sound (Masri et al., 2021; Resnik and Polley, 2021; Resnik and Polley, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and represents a conceptual framework

claim: PyrNs with low spontaneous activity rates and non-monotonic encoding of sound intensity showed more stable gain control after trauma.
source: In particular, PyrNs with low spontaneous activity rates and non-monotonic encoding of sound intensity – features associated with stronger intracortical inhibition (Tan et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2006) – showed more stable gain control after trauma
evidence: Based on predictive modeling results and supported by citations

claim: Initially high spontaneous activity, hyper-correlation, and gradual monotonic intensity growth functions could be reflective of weaker intracortical inhibitory tone and were features that predicted non-homeostatic excess gain after acoustic trauma.
source: Conversely, initially high spontaneous activity, hyper-correlation, and gradual monotonic intensity growth functions could be reflective of weaker intracortical inhibitory tone and were features that predicted non-homeostatic excess gain after acoustic trauma
evidence: Based on predictive modeling results and inference about inhibitory tone

claim: Near-complete elimination of cochlear afferent input was associated with functional deafness at the level of the ACtx in approximately half the animals but a remarkable recovery of sound responsiveness in the other half.
source: In an earlier study, we applied ouabain to the cochlear round window to produce bilateral lesions of approximately 95% of cochlear afferent neurons. Near-complete elimination of cochlear afferent input was associated with functional deafness at the level of the ACtx in approximately half the animals but a remarkable recovery of sound responsiveness in the other half
evidence: Based on prior study by the authors

claim: Mice that recovered sound processing weeks after cochlear neural loss all featured a rapid decline in PV-mediated feedforward inhibition onto PyrNs during the first hours and days following the peripheral injury, while the mice that showed no functional recovery expressed a far slower decay in PV-mediated inhibition.
source: Single unit recordings from the cohort of mice that recovered sound processing weeks after cochlear neural loss all featured a rapid decline in PV-mediated feedforward inhibition onto PyrNs during the first hours and days following the peripheral injury, while the mice that showed no functional recovery expressed a far slower decay in PV-mediated inhibition (Resnik and Polley, 2017)
evidence: Based on prior study by the authors

claim: In marmosets with unilateral cochlear implants, single units with narrowly tuned non-monotonic acoustic frequency-response areas were suppressed by spatially diffuse electrical stimulation of the auditory nerve, while units with broad, V-shaped acoustic selectivity encoded cochlear implant stimulation with high fidelity.
source: Another piece of evidence comes from ACtx single unit recordings in marmosets outfitted with unilateral cochlear implants. Single units with narrowly tuned non-monotonic acoustic frequency-response areas – presumably reflecting stronger local inhibition – were suppressed by spatially diffuse electrical stimulation of the auditory nerve. Conversely, units with broad, V-shaped acoustic selectivity encoded cochlear implant stimulation with high fidelity (Johnson et al., 2016)
evidence: Based on prior study cited

claim: The effects of peripheral afferent perturbations on central circuits are not exclusively determined by bottom-up drive but instead are also brokered by variations in the balance of excitation and inhibition within the local circuit or by gene expression differences between individual cells.
source: Collectively, these findings underscore that the effects of peripheral afferent perturbations on central circuits are not exclusively determined by bottom-up drive but instead are also brokered by variations in the balance of excitation and inhibition within the local circuit or by gene expression differences between individual cells
evidence: Based on synthesis of multiple findings from the study and prior literature

claim: At a global level, mitigating influences on cortical plasticity are shaped by developmental stage and circadian programs.
source: At a global level, these mitigating influences are shaped by developmental stage (Dorrn et al., 2010; Harris et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2010) and circadian programs (Basinou et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: At the level of individual neurons, variations in cortical plasticity may reflect latent differences in genetic subtypes of L2/3 PyrNs or purely stochastic variations in inhibitory tone between different microcircuit milieus.
source: but – at the level of individual neurons – may reflect latent differences in genetic subtypes of L2/3 PyrNs or purely stochastic variations in inhibitory tone between different microcircuit milieus
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the findings

claim: An estimated 14% of adult population continuously perceives a phantom ringing or buzzing sound (i.e., tinnitus).
source: Although overload phenotypes are reported across many sensory modalities, they are most common and debilitating in hearing, where an estimated 14% of adult population continuously perceives a phantom ringing or buzzing sound (i.e., tinnitus) (Shargorodsky et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: 9% of adults report hypersensitivity, distress, or even pain in response to ordinary environmental sounds (i.e., hyperacusis).
source: 9% of adults report hypersensitivity, distress, or even pain in response to ordinary environmental sounds (i.e., hyperacusis) (Pienkowski et al., 2014a; Pienkowski et al., 2014b)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: 9% of adults seek health care for poor hearing in complex listening environments but do not have hearing loss.
source: and 9% of adults seek health care for poor hearing in complex listening environments but do not have hearing loss (Parthasarathy et al., 2020a)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: While each facet of auditory overload can occur without evidence of peripheral dysfunction, they are common in persons with SNHL arising from age- or noise-induced degeneration of cochlear hair cells and cochlear afferent nerve terminals.
source: While each facet of auditory overload can occur without evidence of peripheral dysfunction, they are common in persons with SNHL arising from age- or noise-induced degeneration of cochlear hair cells and cochlear afferent nerve terminals (for review see Auerbach and Gritton, 2022; Herrmann and Butler, 2021b; Noreña, 2011; Zeng, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles

claim: In developing sensory systems, deprivation of peripheral input is registered by central sensory neurons via decreased cytosolic calcium levels, which triggers a cascade of genetic, epigenetic, post-transcriptional, and post-translational processes that collectively adjust the electrical excitability of neurons to restore activity back to the baseline set point range.
source: In developing sensory systems, deprivation of peripheral input is registered by central sensory neurons via decreased cytosolic calcium levels, which triggers a cascade of genetic, epigenetic, post-transcriptional, and post-translational processes that collectively adjust the electrical excitability of neurons to restore activity back to the baseline set point range (for review see Harris and Rubel, 2006; Turrigiano, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles

claim: Compensatory changes in the central auditory pathway can be grouped into three categories: synaptic sensitization via upregulation of receptors for excitatory neurotransmitters, synaptic disinhibition via removal of inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors, and increased intrinsic excitability via changes in the amount and subunit composition of voltage-gated ion channels.
source: Compensatory changes in the central auditory pathway can be grouped into three categories: (1) synaptic sensitization via upregulation of receptors for excitatory neurotransmitters (e.g., AMPA receptor scaling) (Balaram et al., 2019; Kotak et al., 2005; Sturm et al., 2017; Teichert et al., 2017); (2) synaptic disinhibition via removal of inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors (Balaram et al., 2019; Richardson et al., 2013; Sanes and Kotak, 2011; Sarro et al., 2008; Sturm et al., 2017); (3) increased intrinsic excitability via changes in the amount and subunit composition of voltage-gated ion channels that set the resting membrane potential, membrane resistance, and spike 'burstiness' (Li et al., 2015; Li et al., 2013; Pilati et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Neural gain adjustments following adult-onset hearing loss often over-shoot the mark, producing catastrophic downstream consequences at the level of network excitability and sound perception.
source: Whereas homeostatic changes – by definition – restore neural activity to a baseline activity rate following a perturbation (Turrigiano, 2012), neural gain adjustments following adult-onset hearing loss often over-shoot the mark, producing catastrophic downstream consequences at the level of network excitability and sound perception (Eggermont, 2017; Nahmani and Turrigiano, 2014; Noreña, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: With conventional microelectrode recordings, synaptic and intrinsic compensatory processes manifest as increased spontaneous activity rates, increased spike synchrony, steeper slopes of sound intensity growth functions, and poor adaptation to background noise sources.
source: With conventional microelectrode recordings, the synaptic and intrinsic compensatory processes described above manifest as increased spontaneous activity rates, increased spike synchrony, steeper slopes of sound intensity growth functions, and poor adaptation to background noise sources (for recent review see Auerbach and Gritton, 2022; Herrmann and Butler, 2021b)
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles

claim: Hyperactive and hyper-correlated activity in regions of the cortical topographic map corresponding to peripheral sensorineural damage is widely understood to be the underlying neural basis of phantom sound perception in tinnitus.
source: Hyperactive and hyper-correlated activity in regions of the cortical topographic map corresponding to peripheral sensorineural damage is widely understood to be the underlying neural basis of phantom sound perception in tinnitus (Auerbach et al., 2019; Herrmann and Butler, 2021b; Noreña, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: These findings identify a neurophysiological target for testing therapeutic strategies in animals and inform the selection of non-invasive biomarkers for the development of improved diagnostics and therapies in human populations.
source: These findings identify a neurophysiological target for testing therapeutic strategies in animals and inform the selection of non-invasive biomarkers for the development of improved diagnostics and therapies in human populations (Polley and Schiller, 2022)
evidence: Represents implications of the findings with citation
